Amino-acid composition comparison between SaPS (PS-Self) and PdPS (PS-Part) proteins:

1. SaPS proteins are strongly enriched in disorder-promoting residues (Gly 1.44x, Pro 1.30x, Gln 1.25x, Ser 1.20x, Thr 1.20x) and depleted in order-promoting hydrophobic residues (Cys 0.47x, Trp 0.61x, Ile 0.75x, Leu 0.75x) relative to NoPS. Within IDRs, aromatic stickers Tyr (1.81x) and Phe (1.78x) show the strongest enrichment.

2. PdPS proteins show a weaker but qualitatively similar pattern: enriched in Gln (1.15x), Pro (1.10x), Arg (1.10x), Lys (1.08x); depleted in Cys (0.69x), Trp (0.67x), Phe (0.82x). Higher charged-residue content (Arg, Lys, Glu) distinguishes PdPS from SaPS.

3. Direct SaPS vs PdPS: The largest differences are Gly (1.39x higher in SaPS), Thr (1.21x), Pro (1.18x). PdPS is richer in charged residues (Glu, Lys, Arg). SaPS has higher IDR coverage (30.7% vs 21.7%).

4. These patterns are consistent across both the multi-organism and human-only subsets.

Predictor performance:

5. SaPS vs NoPS: All three predictors perform well. PLAAC (AUC=0.834), PScore (AUC=0.831), catGRANULE (AUC=0.817). At Youden-optimal thresholds, recall is 67-73% but precision is ~1% due to extreme class imbalance.

6. PdPS vs NoPS: Performance drops substantially. catGRANULE (AUC=0.706), PScore (AUC=0.663), PLAAC (AUC=0.644). PdPS proteins are harder to predict from sequence alone.

7. SaPS vs PdPS: PLAAC achieves the best discrimination (AUC=0.719), followed by PScore (AUC=0.702), catGRANULE (AUC=0.665). Moderate AUC of 0.66-0.72 confirms that SaPS and PdPS have overlapping but discriminable sequence signatures.

8. Human subset results are consistent with the all-organism analysis.

9. FuzDrop scores were not present in the dataset and could not be evaluated.

Within IDRs, aromatic stickers Tyr (1.81×) and Phe (1.78×) show the strongest enrichment. PdPS shows weaker enrichment with higher charged-residue content (Arg, Lys). SaPS has higher IDR coverage (30.7%) than PdPS (21.7%) or NoPS (12.5%).
